title: Counting the wrong way
summary: Learn how a loop’s update can move away from its stopping condition, how to trace the problem, and how to choose the right direction.
objectives: Explain how a loop’s update changes the value tested by its condition.
Trace a loop to see whether its counter moves toward the stopping condition.
Choose an update that matches the loop’s starting value and condition.
Recognise wrong-direction updates in `for` and `while` loops.

blocks.text: A counting loop needs to move its counter toward the point where its condition becomes false. A common mistake is to move the counter the other way. This loop is meant to print the numbers from 0 to 3:

The condition is `i < 4`, but `i--` makes `i` smaller. The condition stays true instead of stopping when `i` reaches 4. The code compiles: `javac` does not warn that the update goes the wrong way. The problem shows up when the program runs.

blocks.title: A Java detail
blocks.text: This example uses an `int`. Java `int` values eventually wrap around, so this exact loop is not literally endless. It runs for an enormous number of passes before the condition becomes false. That is still a serious bug.

A `for` loop runs its update after the body, then checks its condition again. In this example, `i` starts at 0. The condition asks whether `i` is less than 4, so the loop body runs. But `i--` changes `i` to −1, then −2, and so on. Those values are still less than 4.

blocks.caption: The wrong update keeps the condition true
blocks.mermaid:
flowchart TD
  A[Set i to zero] --> B{Is i less than 4}
  B -- yes --> C[Print i]
  C --> D[Subtract one from i]
  D --> B
  B -- no --> E[Leave the loop]

blocks.title: Check the direction
items: Read the condition: `i < 4` means the loop continues while `i` is below 4.
Read the update: `i--` subtracts 1 from `i` after each pass.
Ask whether the update moves `i` toward a value that makes `i < 4` false. It does not.

sections.title: Trace it, one pass at a time

blocks.text: A trace is a record of a loop’s values, condition checks, and actions. Here are the first passes of the broken loop. The condition remains true because each new value is still less than 4.

blocks.caption: Counter values at the start of the first four passes

blocks.text: The loop does not reach 4 by subtracting 1. For the intended count from 0 up to 3, change the update to `i++`. That adds 1 each time, so the condition eventually becomes false.

The right update depends on the direction of the count. Counting upward usually adds 1. Counting downward usually subtracts 1. In both cases, check that the counter moves toward a value that makes the condition false.

bad.title: Counting upward with a downward update

good.title: Count from 0 up to 3

blocks.note: The condition `i < 4` needs `i` to grow toward 4. The update `i++` adds 1 after each pass. When `i` reaches 4, the condition is false and the loop stops.

bad.title: Counting downward with an upward update

good.title: Count from 3 down to 1

blocks.note: The condition `i >= 1` stays true while `i` is at least 1. To reach a value below 1, subtract 1 with `i--`. Adding 1 moves away from that stopping point.

blocks.text: The same direction check works in other loops too. A `while` loop also repeats while its condition is true. Look at the condition and find which value changes inside the body.

bad.title: A while loop moves away from its stop

good.title: The update moves toward the stop

blocks.note: The loop type changed, but the reasoning did not. With `i < 3`, adding 1 moves `i` toward a value that makes the condition false.

bad.title: A countdown condition with an upward update

good.title: A countdown update matches the condition

blocks.note: For `i > 0`, the loop stops when `i` reaches 0 or less. Subtracting 1 moves toward that point; adding 1 moves away from it.

blocks.question: What update makes this loop count from 1 to 5?
blocks.explanation: The condition `i <= 5` stays true until `i` becomes greater than 5. Adding 1 moves toward that stopping point.

blocks.question: A loop starts at 4 and should count down while `i >= 1`. Which update moves toward the stopping point?
blocks.explanation: The condition becomes false when `i` drops below 1. Subtracting 1 moves toward that value.

blocks.question: What is the main problem with this loop?
options: It moves `i` away from the value that would stop the loop.
It does not have an initial value.
The condition is checked after the body.
blocks.explanation: The condition keeps going while `i` is less than 3. Subtracting 1 makes `i` smaller, so it does not move toward a value that makes the condition false.

items: A loop repeats while its condition is true.
A `for` loop runs its update after the body and before the next condition check.
Match the update to the condition: `i++` moves upward, and `i--` moves downward.
Trace a few passes. Check whether the counter moves toward a value that makes the condition false.
A wrong-direction update usually compiles. The bug appears when the loop runs.
